cells.tense: You're in the middle of keeping what you value alive, and your hand is on it right now.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already tend — a meal, a habit, a story — and offer it to one other person today. Stay long enough to watch how they take it. That handover is the return: you learn which parts of it travel and which parts were only ever yours.
cells.core:
Keeping something alive for others is what you do on an ordinary week: you show up to the meal, the meeting, the call, and you carry the thing forward without making a fuss about it. It doesn't ask much of you because you've been doing it long enough that it's mostly automatic.

What you might try is handing one piece of it over on purpose — pick something you're already tending and offer it to one other person, then stay long enough to watch how they take it. That's the same holding you do naturally, done once where you can see the result. You get to find out which parts of it travel and which parts were only ever yours.
cells.sheetLine: Handing on what you already keep is how you find out what it's worth.
cells.verb: still carrying what you chose to keep alive
cells.place: in what a group hands down as its own

cells.tense: You're bracing for a future where the thing dies if you stop pushing, so you're pushing harder than anyone asked.
cells.ask: Take one piece of the practice you're trying to keep alive — one meeting, one meal, one conversation — and leave it alone for a full day. Say nothing about it to anyone until tomorrow. What that gives back is the difference between what you know about it and what you're afraid will happen.
cells.core:
In a steady stretch you show up, you pass on what you have, and you let the thing land or not land on its own timing. That's not how it's going right now. Right now you're already several steps into a future where something goes wrong, and you're shaping everything you say around that future — rehearsing the defense before anyone's asked, keeping the practice alive by sheer will. The pushing has started to cost you the thing the pushing was for. Leaving one piece of it alone for a day is the way back here.

So take one meeting, one meal, one conversation, and leave it alone for a full day. Say nothing about it to anyone until tomorrow. That gives you back the difference between what you know to be true about it and what you're afraid will happen.
cells.sheetLine: Keeping something alive by force has a way of wearing out the thing you're keeping.
cells.verb: still carrying what you chose to keep alive
cells.place: in what a group hands down as its own

cells.tense: You're standing at a doorway that's already closed behind you, keeping what you value alive in a way that used to work and doesn't.
cells.ask: Write down one practice or story someone passed to you that you've kept to yourself. By this time next week, call one person who'd want it and hand it over in your own words. Watching it land somewhere new can bring back the part of this that comes alive when you pass it on.
cells.core:
You used to carry your share of what your people hand down — you showed up, you kept the thing going, you were someone the others could count on. These days it mostly feels like habit, or obligation, or nothing, and you've pulled back from the part where you're the one keeping it alive for someone else. You still care about it. What's gone quiet is the part where you're the one holding it up.

Pick one thing — a recipe, a habit, a story — that someone passed to you and you've kept to yourself. Give yourself a week, then call one person who'd want it, someone in the group it belongs to or someone well outside it, and hand it over in your own words. Watching it land somewhere new is a way to get back in touch with the part of this that only works when you're handing it on.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you value is waiting for you to hand it to someone.
cells.verb: still carrying what you chose to keep alive

cells.tense: You're already holding something together for the people around you, and you're describing it as if it were holding itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to yourself, that one thing you keep going for the group is yours — that you're the one doing it. Then do one small thing in the next hour that keeps it alive, and notice you did it. The part of this that's been running on its own gets credited to the person who did it.
cells.core:
In a steady stretch you're the one doing the quiet work — showing up early, remembering what to do, keeping something that matters from falling apart — and you know that's what you're doing. Right now it's happening, and you're talking about it like it's just the way things are, or like the group does it, or like it doesn't count. The effort is real. The credit for it hasn't landed anywhere. Saying it's yours is the way back here.

Try saying out loud, to yourself, that one thing you keep going is yours — that you're the one doing it. Then do one small thing in the next hour that keeps it alive, and notice on purpose that you did it. That's not make-work. The part of this that's been running on its own gets to land back on the person who's actually been doing it.
cells.sheetLine: The work is already yours. You're just not the one who's been saying so.
cells.verb: still carrying what you chose to keep alive
cells.place: in what a group hands down as its own

A reader could reasonably say the Balanced cell is praising a method I invented for them, so it has to name a visible act and let them judge it. Every ask has to survive being wrong: something they could do at the table they are at, learn from, and walk away from without me having certified anything about them; the steward's ask is the one I have to watch it does not become caring for others on command. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader in my first draft was the one about the check being returnable — it was the house admiring its own idea.
